messages.content: My search client builds the URL by string concatenation: base + "?q=" + term + "&limit=10". When a user searches for "rock & roll" the results come back wrong — it looks like the search only ran on part of the term. The API itself is fine when I test it from a browser. What is my client doing to the request?

arguments.code:
from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlencode

term = "rock & roll"
naive_url = "https://api.example.test/search?q=" + term + "&limit=10"
print("naive url     :", naive_url)
print("server parsed :", parse_qs(naive_url.split("?", 1)[1]))

fixed_url = "https://api.example.test/search?" + urlencode({"q": term, "limit": 10})
print("fixed url     :", fixed_url)
print("server parsed :", parse_qs(fixed_url.split("?", 1)[1]))

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
The API is innocent — your client is amputating the term. In the naive URL the raw `&` inside "rock & roll" is a parameter separator, so the server parses `q` as just `'rock '` and the rest of the term becomes a stray fragment that `parse_qs` drops entirely. The server never saw the real query.

The fixed version runs the parameters through `urlencode`, which percent-encodes the ampersand as `%26`. Now the server parses `q` back to exactly `'rock & roll'`.

The rule: never interpolate raw user text into a URL. Query strings are a wire format with reserved characters (`&`, `=`, `#`, `+`, spaces), and encoding is not optional decoration. Use your HTTP library's `params=` argument or `urlencode` so every value is encoded exactly once, by construction, instead of hoping user input happens to be URL-safe.

I am creating widgets with a POST. I build the JSON body correctly — I printed it and it is valid JSON — but the server answers 415 Unsupported Media Type and says the body was not parsed. The same body pasted into a test tool works. What differs between my client and the test tool?

arguments.code:
import json

def fake_create(content_type, raw):
    if content_type != "application/json":
        return 415, "unsupported media type: body not parsed as JSON"
    data = json.loads(raw)
    return 201, f"created widget name={data['name']}"

body_text = json.dumps({"name": "gear"})
print("body on the wire:", body_text)
print("sent as text/plain      ->", fake_create("text/plain", body_text))
print("sent as application/json ->", fake_create("application/json", body_text))

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
The body is identical in both runs — only the label changed, and the label is what the server routes on. Your client serialized the dict to a JSON *string* itself and sent it as a raw body, so the transport stamped it `text/plain` (the usual default for string bodies). The server's JSON parser is only wired to the `application/json` content type, so it refused to parse at all: 415, body ignored.

The test tool set the content type correctly, which is why the same bytes worked there.

Fix: stop serializing by hand. Pass the dict to your client's `json=` parameter (or set `Content-Type: application/json` explicitly). Hand-serializing is how the body and its label drift apart — the library keeps them consistent because it does both in one step. When a server says "not parsed", debug the headers before you debug the payload.

After a config refactor, my client 404s on every endpoint. The base URL and the paths did not change, I just split them into a BASE constant and per-call relative paths and joined them with +. Sometimes the joined URL has a double slash, sometimes a segment vanishes. Is the server routing broken?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
/v1//users -> 404 no such route
/v1users -> 404 no such route
/v1/users -> 200 OK
/v1/users -> 200 OK

The server routing is fine; string concatenation is not a URL join. `+` knows nothing about path segments, so `"/v1/" + "/users"` keeps both slashes (`/v1//users`, a different route that 404s) and `"/v1" + "users"` welds the segment on (`/v1users`). Which failure you get depends on which side of the split happened to carry the slash — exactly why the refactor broke "every" endpoint in two different-looking ways.

The fix normalizes the seam: strip trailing slashes from the base and leading slashes from the relative part, then join with exactly one `/`. Both combinations now produce `/v1/users` and a 200.

Better still, use a real join (`urllib.parse.urljoin` with its base-must-end-in-slash rule understood, or your client's base_url handling) — but even the rstrip/lstrip join beats `+`, because it makes the seam invariant instead of config-dependent.

My client sets an Authorization header and an X-Trace header on the shared session. One special call passes its own headers dict to add a one-off token, and from then on the tracing header never reaches the server — but only on that call. My wrapper code merges nothing; it just forwards what it is given. Why does one call lose the session headers?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
replace semantics -> ('Bearer ONEOFF', '<missing>')
merge semantics   -> ('Bearer ONEOFF', 'trace-1')

Nothing is wrong with the server or the session — your wrapper implements replace semantics where you expect merge semantics. When the special call supplies its own headers dict, the wrapper forwards that dict *instead of* the session's, so `X-Trace` silently vanishes for exactly that one call. The Authorization survives only because the one-off dict happens to carry its own.

The merged version starts from the session headers and lets per-request keys override: the one-off token wins for Authorization, and `X-Trace` is still present.

This bug class hides well because most calls pass no headers and inherit everything, so the failure correlates with the *special* call, not with the header itself. Rule for wrappers: per-request headers extend session headers, they never substitute for them — merge with the request winning per-key, and say so in the wrapper's contract.
My filter parameter works in every test tool but my Python client gets a 400: "active must be 'true' or 'false', got 'True'". I am passing a boolean variable. Where does the capital T come from?

arguments.code:
import json

def fake_users(query):
    raw = query.get("active")
    if raw not in ("true", "false"):
        return f"400: active must be 'true' or 'false', got {raw!r}"
    return "200: 3 users" if raw == "true" else "200: 1 user"

active = True
print("str(active)        ->", fake_users({"active": str(active)}))
print("str(active).lower()->", fake_users({"active": str(active).lower()}))
print("json.dumps(active) ->", json.dumps(active))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
str(active)        -> 400: active must be 'true' or 'false', got 'True'
str(active).lower()-> 200: 3 users
json.dumps(active) -> true

The capital T is Python's, not the server's invention. `str(True)` produces `'True'` — Python's spelling — but the API expects JSON spelling, `'true'`. When you format a boolean into a query string by hand, you inherit the host language's representation, and strict APIs reject it.

`json.dumps(True)` shows the wire spelling is `true`. Lowercasing works for this one case, but the durable fix is to never hand-format values: pass the boolean through your client's `params=` dict and let its encoder serialize it, or use `json.dumps` for the value.

Same trap, other costumes: `None` becomes the literal string `'None'` instead of an omitted parameter, and lists become `"['a', 'b']"`. Any time you see a language-flavored literal (`True`, `None`, brackets) in a server error, suspect your serializer, not their parser.

I need items tagged with either of two tags. My client sends tag=a,b in one parameter and gets zero results, but the catalog definitely has items under both tags. Sending the request twice with one tag each works. What is the server actually receiving?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
comma-joined -> (['a,b'], [])
repeated     -> (['a', 'b'], ['a1', 'a2', 'b1'])

The server receives exactly one tag: the literal string `'a,b'`. Comma-joining is a convention *some* APIs document; it is not a URL standard, and this API parses repeated parameters instead. Since no item is tagged `a,b`, the result set is honestly empty — the catalog was never asked for `a` or `b` separately.

The repeated form `tag=a&tag=b` parses to `['a', 'b']` and returns all three items.

How to avoid guessing: check how the API represents a multi-value in its own responses or examples, or test both forms against a known fixture as done here. Client libraries usually take a list value in `params=` and emit the repeated form. The deeper lesson is that "zero results" is a *successful* response to a different question than the one you meant to ask — print the parsed parameters the server saw before concluding the data is missing.

My file-download client works for normal file names, but any file whose ID contains a slash fails with 404, and the logs show the request landing on a 'nested' handler. The files exist. Why does one character in the ID reroute the request?

arguments.code:
from urllib.parse import quote

def fake_route(path):
    parts = [p for p in path.split("/") if p]
    if len(parts) == 2 and parts[0] == "files":
        return f"200: serving file id={parts[1]}"
    return f"404: no single-file route matches {len(parts)} segments"

print(fake_route("/files/report.pdf"))
print(fake_route("/files/a/b"))
print(fake_route("/files/" + quote("a/b", safe="")))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
200: serving file id=report.pdf
404: no single-file route matches 3 segments
200: serving file id=a%2Fb

Because in a path, `/` is not data — it is structure. The ID `a/b` pasted raw into the path turns one segment into two, the router counts three segments, matches a different (or no) route, and 404s. The file was never looked up; the request was misshapen before routing began.

Percent-encoding the segment with `quote(..., safe="")` turns the slash into `%2F`, so the path keeps two segments and the server decodes the ID back to `a/b` after routing. Note `safe=""` matters: `quote`'s default leaves `/` unescaped precisely because it assumes path text.

Same family: IDs containing `?`, `#`, or `%` corrupt query, fragment, and encoding respectively. Path parameters are user data wearing a structural costume — encode them as segments, always, even when today's IDs look tame.

I switched my create call from a test tool to my Python client and now the server rejects half my fields: quantities arrive as the string '3.0' and a nested object arrives as gibberish. In the test tool I sent JSON. In the client I passed the same dict to the data= argument. What did data= do to my payload?

arguments.code:
import json
from urllib.parse import parse_qs

def fake_create(content_type, raw):
    if content_type == "application/json":
        d = json.loads(raw)
        return f"201: name={d['name']} qty={d['qty']} ({type(d['qty']).__name__})"
    fields = parse_qs(raw)
    return f"400: qty must be an integer, got {fields.get('qty')}"

payload = {"name": "gear", "qty": 3}
# data= form-encodes: values are stringified, so 3 left the process as part of a form body
print(fake_create("application/x-www-form-urlencoded", "name=gear&qty=3.0"))
print(fake_create("application/json", json.dumps(payload)))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
400: qty must be an integer, got ['3.0']
201: name=gear qty=3 (int)

`data=` and `json=` are different serializers. `data=` form-encodes the dict: every value is flattened to a string (numbers lose their type, nested objects become their `repr`), and the content type becomes `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. The server parsed the form faithfully and still rejected it, because `qty` arrived as text — in this fake, wearing a `.0` from a float upstream — instead of a JSON integer.

With `json=`, the same dict crosses as `{"name": "gear", "qty": 3}` with the JSON content type, and the server sees a real integer.

The diagnostic habit: when a server complains about field *types* on a request that "sends the same dict", capture the raw body and content type. The dict in your code is not the payload; the payload is whatever the serializer made of it.

My client parses the response with json.loads and intermittently gets a decode error: 'Expecting value: line 1 column 1'. The endpoint returns JSON when I check it manually. The failures cluster around busy periods. What else could the body be?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
Accept=None: JSONDecodeError - body was application/xml: <total>3</total>
Accept='application/json': parsed total=3

The body was XML. With no `Accept` header, this server defaults to its legacy format, and `json.loads` fails on `<total>...` at the very first character — hence "line 1 column 1", the signature of parsing the wrong format entirely, not of corrupt JSON.

The intermittency is the tell: under load, a proxy or a fallback path may drop or ignore your usual headers, or a different backend answers. Manually, you (or your test tool) were sending `Accept: application/json` all along.

Two fixes, both cheap: always send an explicit `Accept: application/json`, and in the client, check the response's content type before parsing — log the actual type and the first bytes when it is not JSON. That converts a cryptic decode error into a one-line diagnosis. Never let the parser be your format detector.

Downloads fail for files with spaces in the name. I fixed it by percent-encoding the name before handing it to my client helper — and now it fails differently: the server says the file 'my%20file.txt' does not exist. Encoding it broke it. What is happening?

arguments.code:
from urllib.parse import quote, unquote

name = "my file.txt"
once = quote(name)
twice = quote(once)
print("client sends (encoded twice):", twice)
print("server decodes once, looks up:", unquote(twice))
print("actual file name             :", name)
print("lookup succeeds:", unquote(twice) == name)
print("encoded once, lookup succeeds:", unquote(once) == name)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
client sends (encoded twice): my%2520file.txt
server decodes once, looks up: my%20file.txt
actual file name             : my file.txt
lookup succeeds: False
encoded once, lookup succeeds: True

You encoded an already-encoded value. Your helper was *already* percent-encoding the name, so your manual `quote` produced `my%20file.txt`, and the helper encoded the `%` again into `%25`, sending `my%2520file.txt`. The server decodes exactly once — correctly — and looks up a file literally named `my%20file.txt`, which does not exist.

Encoding must happen exactly once across the whole pipeline, which means you must know which layer owns it. If the helper encodes, pass raw text. If you build URLs by hand, you own encoding — all of it.

The fingerprint of double-encoding in logs is `%25` (an encoded percent sign) or names that look "half-decoded". When a fix makes a bug change shape instead of disappearing, count how many times each transformation is applied; stacked fixes are a common way to get to two.

My nightly export collects zero records and reports success. The API paginates with a page parameter and holds 30 records. My loop starts at page 0 and stops when a page comes back empty. The API docs are ambiguous about the first page. Reproduce my loop against a stand-in and tell me what is wrong.

arguments.code:
ITEMS = list(range(1, 31))

def fake_page(page, size=10):
    if page < 1:
        return []  # this API is 1-based: page 0 is not an error, just empty
    start = (page - 1) * size
    return ITEMS[start:start + size]

def fetch_all(first_page):
    got, page = [], first_page
    while True:
        chunk = fake_page(page)
        if not chunk:
            break
        got += chunk
        page += 1
    return got

print("starting at page 0:", len(fetch_all(0)), "records")
print("starting at page 1:", len(fetch_all(1)), "records")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
starting at page 0: 0 records
starting at page 1: 30 records

Your loop is well-formed and your stop condition is reasonable — the contract underneath it is not what you assumed. This API is 1-based, and page 0 returns an empty list rather than an error. Starting at 0, the very first fetch is empty, your loop reads that as "end of data", and the export succeeds with zero records.

Starting at page 1 collects all 30.

The nasty part is the API's politeness: an out-of-range page and the end-of-data page look identical, so a wrong start is indistinguishable from an empty dataset. Defenses: treat "zero records on the first page" as a smell worth one probe (fetch page 1 explicitly, or check any total the API offers), and pin the first-page convention in a contract test against a fixture with known contents. Silent-empty is the most expensive success there is.

My paginated pull returns more rows than exist: the source has 25 items, my result has 27, and finance says some rows are duplicated. My loop advances the offset by limit - 1 'to be safe against gaps'. Show me what that safety costs.

arguments.code:
ITEMS = list(range(1, 26))

def fake_offset(offset, limit):
    return ITEMS[offset:offset + limit]

def fetch_all(step, limit=10):
    got, offset = [], 0
    while offset < len(ITEMS):
        got += fake_offset(offset, limit)
        offset += step
    return got

buggy = fetch_all(step=9)
fixed = fetch_all(step=10)
print("step=limit-1:", len(buggy), "rows,", len(set(buggy)), "unique")
print("duplicated ids:", sorted(i for i in set(buggy) if buggy.count(i) > 1))
print("step=limit  :", len(fixed), "rows,", len(set(fixed)), "unique")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
step=limit-1: 27 rows, 25 unique
duplicated ids: [10, 19]
step=limit  : 25 rows, 25 unique

The "safety" overlap is the bug. Advancing by `limit - 1` makes each page re-fetch the last item of the previous page as the first item of the next, so ids 10 and 19 each appear twice: 27 rows, 25 unique. There were no gaps to protect against — offset pagination over a static list has no holes; consecutive pages tile exactly when the step equals the page size.

Stepping by `limit` returns 25 rows, all unique.

Overlapping windows are a legitimate technique for *time-window* queries over data that can shift mid-scan, where you dedupe afterward. Applied blindly to offset pagination, the overlap just manufactures duplicates. And the cheap audit that caught this — compare `len(result)` against `len(set(result))` before shipping — belongs in every paginated pull. Finance should never be your duplicate detector.

Our inventory sync uses offset pagination over a live table. On busy days the result has duplicates AND misses items, even though every page request succeeds. On quiet days it is perfect. The API offers cursor pagination too, which we do not use. Explain the busy-day corruption with a stand-in.

arguments.code:
store = [f"item-{i}" for i in range(1, 21)]

def fake_offset(offset, limit):
    return store[offset:offset + limit]

# busy day: two new items are inserted at the front between page fetches
page1 = fake_offset(0, 10)
store[0:0] = ["item-new1", "item-new2"]
page2 = fake_offset(10, 10)
got = page1 + page2
print("collected:", len(got), "unique:", len(set(got)))
print("duplicated:", sorted(i for i in set(got) if got.count(i) > 1))
print("missed    :", sorted(set(f"item-{i}" for i in range(1, 21)) - set(got)))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
collected: 20 unique: 18
duplicated: ['item-10', 'item-9']
missed    : ['item-19', 'item-20']

Offset pagination addresses rows by *position*, and positions move. The two inserts at the front shifted every existing item two slots later, so the second page (offset 10) re-read the last two items of page 1 — duplicates — and the items pushed past the second page's window were never read at all — misses. Quiet days have no inserts, so the same code looks correct.

No page request failed; the scan's frame of reference moved underneath it. This is inherent to offset/limit over mutating data, not a server bug.

Fixes, in order of strength: use the cursor pagination the API offers (a cursor pins identity, not position); or snapshot first (read a total/ID list, then fetch by ID); or, if you must offset-scan a live table, scan in a stable sort order and dedupe + reconcile counts, treating the result as approximate. Pick based on whether the consumer can tolerate approximate — a sync feeding finance cannot.

My cursor-paginated import hung in staging and had to be killed. The logs show it fetched thousands of pages. The dataset has 40 items. I initialize the cursor once before the loop and pass it on every request. What will the request log show?

arguments.code:
DATA = list(range(1, 41))

def fake_cursor(cursor, size=10):
    start = 0 if cursor is None else cursor
    chunk = DATA[start:start + size]
    nxt = start + size if start + size < len(DATA) else None
    return chunk, nxt

# buggy client: cursor initialized once, never reassigned inside the loop
cursor = None
calls = []
for _ in range(6):  # safety bound standing in for the kill
    chunk, nxt = fake_cursor(cursor)
    calls.append((cursor, len(chunk)))
print("requests (cursor sent, rows back):", calls)

cursor, total = None, 0
while True:
    chunk, cursor = fake_cursor(cursor)
    total += len(chunk)
    if cursor is None:
        break
print("fixed client collected:", total)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
requests (cursor sent, rows back): [(None, 10), (None, 10), (None, 10), (None, 10), (None, 10), (None, 10)]
fixed client collected: 40

The log will show the same request forever: cursor `None`, first page, ten rows, thousands of times. You initialize the cursor before the loop but never assign the response's `next_cursor` back to it, so every iteration restarts the walk. The loop's other exit — the dataset ending — is unreachable because the first page always promises a next page. Only the kill stopped it.

The fixed version threads the returned cursor into the next request and terminates when the API says there is no next page: 40 items, four requests.

Cursor loops have exactly two moving parts — advance the cursor, stop on the sentinel — and both live in the loop body. A cheap guard while developing: log the cursor per request and cap total pages at something like `expected_items / page_size * 2`. A repeated identical cursor in the log is this bug's fingerprint.

My page walker crashes near the end of every large export with 'expected a full page, got 7'. I added that assertion myself to catch truncation. The API returns 47 items in pages of 20. Why does my own safety check fire on healthy data?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
strict walker died: expected a full page, got 7
lenient walker: 47 items

Your assertion encodes a false invariant: only the *last* page may be short, and it almost always is. 47 items in pages of 20 is 20 + 20 + 7 — the 7 is not truncation, it is the remainder, the normal signature of a healthy final page. The strict walker dies after successfully fetching everything, mistaking the finish line for a failure.

The lenient walker treats "short page" as the termination signal and returns all 47.

If you want a truncation check, assert on something that can actually distinguish it: a server-reported total (`collected == total`), sequential IDs with no gaps, or a checksum. Asserting page fullness checks a property the protocol never promised. Safety checks built on imagined invariants are worse than none — they convert success into a crash at the worst moment, after the work is done.

To speed up a backfill I fetch pages in parallel workers that share a 'next page' counter. The result is missing an entire page and has another page twice, though each worker's code is identical to my sequential version. The workers pull the next page number from the shared counter when they start a fetch. Reproduce the race in slow motion.

arguments.code:
PAGES = {1: "a", 2: "b", 3: "c", 4: "d"}
counter = {"next": 1}
fetched = []

def claim():
    n = counter["next"]
    counter["next"] += 1
    return n

# two workers, two rounds each - slow-motion interleaving
p = claim(); fetched.append(PAGES[p])   # worker 1 fetches page 1
p2 = claim()                            # worker 2 claims page 2...
fetched.append(PAGES[p2])               # ...fetches it, but its completion ack is lost
p = claim(); fetched.append(PAGES[p])   # worker 1 fetches page 3
fetched.append(PAGES[p2])               # the supervisor re-runs page 2: fetched TWICE
print("pages fetched:", fetched)
print("pages never fetched:", sorted(set(PAGES.values()) - set(fetched)))
print("pages fetched twice:", sorted(x for x in set(fetched) if fetched.count(x) > 1))
print("claims made:", counter["next"] - 1, "of", len(PAGES), "pages")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
pages fetched: ['a', 'b', 'c', 'b']
pages never fetched: ['d']
pages fetched twice: ['b']
claims made: 3 of 4 pages

The race lives in the gaps between *claiming*, *fetching*, and *acknowledging*. In this interleaving, page 2 is fetched but its completion ack is lost, so the supervisor re-runs it — page 2 lands twice — while the claim budget runs out before page 4 is ever claimed. The result set has a duplicate and a hole, and every individual fetch returned 200. Sequential code cannot produce this because claim, fetch, and record are one indivisible step.

The robust pattern removes the race from the design: partition the page range up front (worker 1 owns pages 1–2, worker 2 owns 3–4), so each page has exactly one owner and a retry re-fetches its *own* page. If pages cannot be known in advance, reconcile at the end: expected page set vs completed page set, and treat any difference as a failed export, not a slightly short one.

Parallelizing a stateful walk is a redesign, not a speedup flag. The completion audit is what turns this class of race from silent data loss into a loud, retryable error.

My client requests limit=500 per page and advances the offset by 500. It silently skips most of the catalog: the API caps page size at 100 but still returns 200. I never see an error. Where did 400 items per page go?

arguments.code:
ITEMS = list(range(1, 1001))

def fake_list(offset, limit):
    effective = min(limit, 100)  # server cap, applied silently
    return {"items": ITEMS[offset:offset + effective], "limit_used": effective}

got, offset = [], 0
while offset < len(ITEMS):
    resp = fake_list(offset, 500)
    got += resp["items"]
    offset += 500  # client advances by what it ASKED for
print("client collected:", len(got), "of", len(ITEMS))
print("server said limit_used:", resp["limit_used"])

got, offset = [], 0
while offset < len(ITEMS):
    resp = fake_list(offset, 500)
    got += resp["items"]
    offset += len(resp["items"])  # advance by what ARRIVED
print("fixed client collected:", len(got))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
client collected: 200 of 1000
server said limit_used: 100
fixed client collected: 1000

Nowhere — they were never sent. The server honored each request with its cap of 100 items, and your client advanced the offset by the 500 it *requested*, striding over items 101–500, 601–1000's predecessors, and so on. It collected 200 of 1000 with every request returning 200. Silent clamping plus assumed advancement is a data-loss machine.

The fix is one line of humility: advance by `len(returned_items)`, not by the requested limit. The fixed loop collects all 1000 regardless of the cap. The response even told the truth — `limit_used: 100` — but metadata you never read cannot save you.

General rule: in pagination, the only trustworthy numbers are the ones in the response (items received, next cursor, reported total). Requested values are intentions. Any loop that advances on intentions will eventually stride past data an API declined to give it.

My export makes 30 page requests for a 30-item dataset with page size 10, and my rate-limit budget hates it. The response JSON has both 'count' and 'pages' fields. My loop runs while page <= response['count']. What am I misreading?

arguments.code:
def fake_page(page):
    return {"items": list(range(10)), "count": 30, "pages": 3, "page": page}

calls = 0
page = 1
while page <= 30:  # 'count' misread as the page count
    resp = fake_page(page)
    calls += 1
    page += 1
print("buggy loop requests:", calls)

calls, page = 0, 1
while page <= fake_page(page)["pages"]:
    calls += 1
    page += 1
print("loop over 'pages':", calls)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buggy loop requests: 30
loop over 'pages': 3

You are looping over the item count as if it were the page count. `count: 30` is items; `pages: 3` is pages. The buggy loop makes 30 requests — 27 of them fetch pages beyond the end (most APIs return empty pages there, so nothing crashes; you just burn rate budget and time).

Looping to `pages` makes the correct 3 requests.

Envelope fields are a dialect per API: `count`, `total`, `total_items`, `total_pages`, `pages` — near-identical names with different meanings, and no error will ever tell you that you picked the wrong one, because every request you make is individually valid. The defense is a fixture test: build a fake with a known shape (30 items, size 10, 3 pages) and assert your walker makes exactly 3 calls and returns 30 items. Field-semantics bugs only show up against known numbers.

Long exports against our CRM die about ten minutes in with 410 Gone on the cursor, and my client's recovery is to restart the whole walk — which then produces duplicates in the target table. The cursor clearly expires. What recovery does not duplicate?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content: (40, 'completed')

Restarting the walk is fine; restarting your *bookkeeping* is what duplicates. When the cursor dies (here, after three uses — real ones expire on time or use count), the recovery above restarts pagination from the beginning but keeps the `seen` set, filtering re-fetched items against everything already emitted. The walk completes with exactly 40 unique items and no duplicates downstream.

Your current client throws away its progress state along with the cursor, so the target table receives the first pages twice.

Two refinements for production: make the sink idempotent as well (upsert by ID), so even a buggy recovery cannot duplicate — defense in depth at both ends; and if the API offers it, prefer resuming from a cheaper anchor (a last-seen ID with `starting_after`) over a full restart. The design principle: pagination state is disposable, emitted-state is not. Keep them in separate variables with separate lifetimes.

The API I use paginates only through Link headers — each response carries an opaque 'next' URL. My client ignores headers and constructs ?page=2, ?page=3 itself, which 404s. My teammate says just parse the header. Show me what following the link looks like against a stand-in, and why constructing URLs was doomed.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
constructed page=2 -> 404
following Link headers collected: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

It was doomed because the cursor is opaque state, not a page number. `Ab3f` and `Zz90` encode server-side position (a snapshot, a signed token, a shard) that cannot be synthesized by incrementing anything — `?page=2` names a parameter this API does not implement, so it 404s.

Following the header works: start at the entry URL, extract the `rel="next"` target, and keep going until a response has no next link. Five items, three requests, zero constructed URLs.

Opaque means opaque: do not parse, increment, cache across runs, or log-and-replay cursors beyond their lifetime. The client's whole job is to carry the token from response to next request untouched. When an API offers both page parameters and Link headers, prefer the headers — they are the mechanism the server actually maintains, and page parameters are often a legacy shim with subtly different behavior.

A customer was charged twice for one order. Our logs show the first POST /orders timed out on our side, the client retried, and both orders exist. The API supports an Idempotency-Key header that we do not send. Walk me through the failure and the fix against a fake server.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
attempt 1: timed out, retrying
no key   -> orders created: 2
attempt 1: timed out, retrying
with key -> orders created: 1

The timeout lied by omission: the request *arrived and was processed* — only the response was lost. From the client's chair, "timeout" means "outcome unknown", not "did not happen". Retrying a non-idempotent POST on an unknown outcome is a second order, faithfully created by a healthy server. Your logs and the customer's statement agree with each other; the API did nothing wrong.

With an `Idempotency-Key`, the retry carries the same key (`checkout-8842`), the server recognizes the replay, returns the original order, and creates nothing new: one order.

Rules to keep: generate one key per *logical operation* (per checkout, not per attempt) and reuse it across that operation's retries; never retry a non-idempotent request without one when money or records move; and treat every timeout on a mutating call as an ambiguity to resolve — by key, or by querying for the outcome — not as a failure to blindly repeat.

Our error logs show one user request generating six identical 400 responses over about a minute. The request had a malformed field, so the 400 was correct every time. Our retry wrapper retries 'any failed request' up to 5 times. What should it actually retry?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
malformed request -> status, attempts: (400, 6)
server saw the same bad payload 6 times
retryable statuses: [429, 500, 502, 503, 504]
400 in retryable set: False

A 400 is the server saying "this request, exactly as written, will never work" — and your wrapper answered by sending it five more times, verbatim. Deterministic failures do not heal with repetition; the minute of retries bought nothing but log noise and rate-limit spend.

The retryable set is about *transience*: 429 (wait and retry), and 5xx (the server's side may recover), plus transport errors where the outcome is unknown. Client errors — 400, 401, 403, 404, 422 — are verdicts on the request or the credentials; retrying them unchanged is always wrong. (A single retry *after changing something* — refreshing a token on 401, fixing a field on 400 — is not a retry, it is a new attempt.)

Encode the policy by status class in the wrapper, with the retryable set explicit and small. "Retry any failure" is not a resilience strategy; it is an amplifier pointed at your own bugs.

Once a week our sync job hangs forever — no error, no progress — and someone kills it in the morning. The API call has no timeout configured anywhere. I cannot reproduce the hang locally. Model it for me: what does 'no timeout' actually wait on?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
with timeout=30: gave up after 30 ticks
with timeout=None: still waiting at tick 1,000,000,000 - the job's 'hang'

"No timeout" waits on the server's goodwill, forever. The connection succeeded, the request was sent, and the peer then went silent — crashed mid-response, deadlocked, or is behind a proxy holding the socket open. TCP will not rescue you on any human timescale. Your weekly hang is a silent server meeting a patient client, and it cannot be reproduced locally because your local fake always answers.

The model shows the whole story: with `timeout=30` the call fails loudly after 30 ticks and the job can retry, skip, or alert. With `None`, the only exit is the latency itself — a billion ticks.

Every network call gets a timeout, no exceptions, sized to the endpoint (a report endpoint earns more than a lookup). Also set a *total* deadline for the job, because per-call timeouts still allow a pathological retry loop to run all night. A hang is the worst failure mode precisely because it produces no signal; a timeout converts it into an ordinary, loggable error.

I implemented exponential backoff as delay = 2 ** attempt, intending milliseconds. During an outage last night the client waited over half an hour between two attempts and the job missed its window. Print my delay sequence and a sane one, and tell me where the half hour came from.

arguments.code:
def buggy_delays(attempts=11):
    return [2 ** a for a in range(1, attempts + 1)]  # meant ms, used as SECONDS

def sane_delays(attempts=6, base=0.5, cap=30):
    return [min(cap, base * 2 ** a) for a in range(attempts)]

b = buggy_delays()
s = sane_delays()
print("buggy delays (s):", b, "total:", sum(b))
print("sane delays  (s):", s, "total:", sum(s))
print("longest buggy wait:", max(b), "s =", max(b) // 60, "min")

messages.content:
Your formula was exponential in the wrong unit. `2 ** attempt` as *milliseconds* would be a gentle 2, 4, 8… ms; consumed as seconds it is 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 — and the sequence keeps doubling past any useful bound because there is no cap. The half hour is just the tail of an uncapped exponential doing exactly what exponentials do.

The sane version has three properties yours lacks: a base in one declared unit (0.5 s), a cap (30 s — beyond this, waiting longer rarely changes the outcome), and usually jitter in production, so thousands of clients failing together do not retry in lockstep and re-crush the recovering server.

Backoff bugs hide because the first two delays look fine in testing; the damage lives at attempt 5+. When you write a backoff, print the full sequence and the total for your max attempts — ten seconds of arithmetic that would have caught this before the outage did.

During last week's outage our monitoring showed the API receiving roughly 9x our normal request volume, and the outage lasted longer than the vendor's fix. We have a gateway that retries 3 times, and each service's client retries 3 times. Do the math for me — where does 9x come from?

arguments.code:
normal_rps = 200
client_retries = 3   # each service client: 1 initial + up to 3 retries is NOT the setting...
gateway_retries = 3

# actual settings found: retries are ATTEMPTS multipliers per layer
per_request_at_gateway = 1 + gateway_retries   # 4 attempts leave the gateway
per_gateway_attempt_at_client = 1 + client_retries  # each spawns 4 client attempts

total = normal_rps * per_request_at_gateway  # gateway layer alone
print("gateway layer alone:", total, "rps equivalent attempts")
print("if both layers multiply:", normal_rps * per_request_at_gateway * per_gateway_attempt_at_client)
print("observed ~9x of", normal_rps, "=", normal_rps * 9)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
gateway layer alone: 800 rps equivalent attempts
if both layers multiply: 3200
observed ~9x of 200 = 1800

Retries multiply across layers — that is the whole story. One user request makes the gateway try up to 4 times (1 + 3 retries). If the client's 4 attempts sit *inside* each gateway attempt, the ceiling is 4 × 4 = 16 attempts per user request; your observed ~9x is that multiplication partially realized (not every attempt always fires, caches absorb some). Meanwhile every attempt lands on a server that is already down, and the flood keeps it down after the fix ships — the outage outlives its cause.

The rule: retry at exactly ONE layer — usually the one closest to the failure, with the full context — and make inner layers fail fast. If two layers must retry, the budgets multiply, so divide them deliberately (e.g., 2 × 2, capped totals, with backoff and jitter at the single effective layer).

Audit for this by counting attempts per user request in logs, per layer. Nobody configures 9x on purpose; it is what independent, locally-reasonable retry settings compose into.

The API returns 503 with a Retry-After header during deploys. My client retries on a fixed 1-second schedule regardless. Deploys last about a minute, and my client burns all 5 retries before the API is back, then fails the job. Show me the two timelines.

arguments.code:
def run(policy, retry_after=20, attempts_allowed=5):
    t, log = 0, []
    for attempt in range(1, attempts_allowed + 1):
        back = t >= 60  # API returns at t=60
        log.append((attempt, t, "200" if back else "503"))
        if back:
            break
        t += retry_after if policy == "honor-header" else 1
    return log

print("fixed 1s     :", run("fixed"))
print("honor header :", run("honor-header"))

messages.content:
Same server, same outage length — the policy decides. The fixed 1-second schedule makes all five attempts inside the first five seconds of a 60-second deploy window: five 503s, budget exhausted, job failed, all before the API even had a chance to return.

Honoring `Retry-After: 20` spaces the attempts to t=0, 20, 40, 60 — and the fourth attempt lands exactly as the API comes back: 200.

`Retry-After` is the server telling you its recovery horizon; a fixed schedule is you guessing instead. Parse it on 429 and 503 (it can be seconds or an HTTP-date), combine it with your own cap so a huge value does not park the job forever, and count the *wait* against the job's total deadline. Retrying sooner than the server asks is not eagerness, it is self-sabotage with extra requests.

My client sets a single global timeout of 1 second for every call. Lookups are fine, but the monthly report endpoint — which legitimately takes about 3 seconds — has literally never succeeded through my client, and its retries triple the load on the busiest endpoint we call. Model why 'one timeout for everything' fails here.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
/lookup -> 200
/search -> 200
/report -> /report needs 15 ticks, timeout is 5 | retries would repeat this 3x per job

A timeout is a claim about how long a *specific* operation may legitimately take, and one global value makes that claim wrong somewhere. Your 1-second budget (5 ticks in the model's scale) is generous for lookups and impossible for the report endpoint, which needs 15 ticks — three times the budget — of honest work. It does not fail sometimes; it fails *always*, deterministically — and because the failure looks like a timeout, your retry policy helpfully fires it three times, tripling load on the most expensive endpoint you call, in exchange for a guaranteed-identical outcome.

Set timeouts per endpoint or per call class, from measured latency (a healthy p99 plus headroom), not from a global constant. And let the failure mode teach you: an endpoint that times out at 100% across days is not flaky, it is mis-budgeted — that pattern in metrics should page the client owner, not trigger more retries.

My upload client retries a failed POST and the server says the second attempt's body is empty — 0 bytes — even though the first attempt sent the full file. The body is a generator that streams the file in chunks. Why does the retry send nothing?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
attempt 1 received bytes: 23
attempt 2 received bytes: 0
with a body factory, attempt 2: 23

Because a generator is a one-way cursor, and attempt 1 consumed it. Joining the stream drained all three chunks; the retry passes the *same generator object*, which is now exhausted, so the join produces zero bytes — a well-formed, empty body that the server truthfully reports.

This bites any single-use body: generators, file objects read to EOF, network streams. The client cannot rewind what it does not own.

Fixes: build the body through a *factory* — a callable the retry loop invokes per attempt to get a fresh stream (shown above) — or buffer small bodies to bytes before the first attempt so retries replay the buffer. Streaming exists to avoid buffering; the factory keeps that benefit. Design rule for retryable clients: anything the attempt consumes must be re-creatable per attempt — bodies, signed headers with timestamps, and idempotency keys scoped per operation rather than per try.

When our payment API goes down, every user request still tries it three times with retries, so the dashboard shows thousands of failed calls and our other work starves. A colleague suggested a circuit breaker. Model the call counts with and without one.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
no breaker   : 200 calls to the dead API
with breaker : 8 calls, the rest failed fast locally

Without a breaker: 50 user requests × 4 attempts = 200 calls hammering an API that is already down, each waiting on timeouts, each logging a failure, and all of them competing with healthy work. The retries cannot succeed — the outage is not a per-request flakiness — they only amplify cost.

With a breaker, the first few failures (threshold 5 attempts here) trip it open, and the remaining user requests fail *fast and locally* with zero network calls: 8 calls total in this model, then silence until a probe tests recovery.

A breaker is an admission that failure can be *correlated*: when a dependency is down, per-request retry logic is the wrong tool, and the kindest thing a client can do — for itself and for the recovering server — is stop calling. Pair it with a half-open probe on a timer so recovery is detected without a flood. Dashboards should chart breaker state alongside call volume; "thousands of failed calls" is often a missing breaker, not a big outage.

After a 2-minute outage, about 200 of our workers all retry at the same moments — exactly 5s, 10s, 20s after failure — and the recovering API falls over twice more before stabilizing. Our backoff is textbook exponential. What is missing, and what does adding it do to the retry timeline?

arguments.code:
import random

WORKERS = 200

def retry_ticks(jitter, seed=7):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    ticks = []
    for _ in range(WORKERS):
        delay = 5  # first backoff step, seconds
        if jitter:
            delay = rng.uniform(0, 5)
        ticks.append(round(delay, 1))
    return ticks

plain = retry_ticks(jitter=False)
print("no jitter: distinct first-retry times:", sorted(set(plain)), "| workers at that tick:", len(plain))
jit = retry_ticks(jitter=True)
from collections import Counter
busiest = Counter(jit).most_common(1)[0]
print("full jitter: busiest single tick holds", busiest[1], "of", WORKERS, "workers")

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
no jitter: distinct first-retry times: [5] | workers at that tick: 200
full jitter: busiest single tick holds 10 of 200 workers

What is missing is randomness — your workers are synchronized. They all failed at the same moment (the outage), they all run the same deterministic backoff, so they all retry at the same instants: 200 workers arriving as one 200-wide spike at 5s, 10s, 20s. A recovering server that could handle a spread-out load gets hit by a battering ram, twice.

Full jitter — drawing each delay uniformly from `[0, backoff]` — decorrelates them. In this run, the busiest single tick holds a handful of workers instead of all 200; the retries smear across the window and the server survives its own recovery.

Deterministic backoff is only safe for a single client. The moment a fleet shares a dependency, jitter is not polish, it is load control. Common recipes: full jitter (`uniform(0, cap)`) or equal jitter (`cap/2 + uniform(0, cap/2)`). And seed your mental model from the fleet's perspective: any behavior that is rational for one client can be a DDoS when ten thousand copies do it simultaneously.

My dashboard job crashes with KeyError: 'data' a few times a week, always at night, and rerunning it in the morning works. The stack trace points at my parsing line, response.json()['data']. The API returns either a data envelope or an error envelope. Show me the crash and the correct first move on any response.

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
The crash is a parsing assumption meeting an error body. At night your token expires; the API correctly returns 403 with an *error* envelope that has no `data` key, and `body["data"]` raises a KeyError whose message ('data') tells you nothing about the actual cause (an auth failure). The morning rerun works because someone or something re-authenticated — the data path was never broken.

The correct first move on *any* response is to branch on status before touching the payload: errors get parsed as errors (`error.code` is the actionable fact), success bodies get parsed as data. The KeyError cost you the real error message — the server told you exactly what was wrong and your client threw it away.

House rule: `response.json()` is step two. Step one is always "what did the status say, and if it failed, what did the error body say?" Log status + error code on every failure and most 'mystery crashes' become one-line diagnoses.

Three endpoints I consume represent 'no results' three different ways, and my shared handler len(response['items']) crashes on two of them. The representations are: an empty list, a null, and the key absent entirely. Write the normalization you would ship and prove it against all three.

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
response 0: naive -> 0
response 1: naive -> TypeError: object of type 'NoneType' has no len()
response 2: naive -> KeyError: 'items'
normalized counts: [0, 0, 0]

All three bodies mean the same thing — zero items — and the naive handler survives only one: `len(None)` is a TypeError, and the missing key is a KeyError. The crashes are not data problems; they are three dialects of emptiness that real APIs genuinely mix, often across endpoints of the same API.

The normalization `resp.get("items") or []` collapses all three to an empty list: `.get` handles absence, and `or` maps both `None` and `[]` to `[]`. Counts come out `[0, 0, 0]` and downstream code sees one shape.

Two cautions. First, normalize at the client boundary, once — do not sprinkle `.get(...) or []` through business logic. Second, `or` also swallows other falsy values; for a field that could legitimately be `0` or `False`, test `is None` explicitly instead. Emptiness dialects are a contract detail worth pinning in a fixture test per endpoint, because the day an API adds a fourth dialect, you want a failing test, not a 3 a.m. crash.

My price-sorted report is wrong: 9-dollar items appear after 100-dollar items. The API returns prices as strings, my code does sorted(items, key=lambda x: x['price']). The data looks right when I print it. Reproduce the ordering and explain it.

arguments.code:
items = [{"name": "a", "price": "9.99"},
         {"name": "b", "price": "100.00"},
         {"name": "c", "price": "20.50"}]

by_string = sorted(items, key=lambda x: x["price"])
print("as strings:", [(i["name"], i["price"]) for i in by_string])
by_value = sorted(items, key=lambda x: float(x["price"]))
print("as numbers:", [(i["name"], i["price"]) for i in by_value])
print("'10' < '9' as strings:", "10" < "9")

messages.content:
Your sort is perfect — for strings. Lexicographic order compares character by character, so `"100.00"` sorts before `"20.50"` which sorts before `"9.99"`, because `'1' < '2' < '9'`. The output shows it plainly: 100, 20, 9.99 — correct string order, nonsense price order. The one-liner at the end is the whole bug in miniature: `"10" < "9"` is `True`.

JSON APIs emit numbers-as-strings more often than you'd expect (money especially, to dodge float issues on their side), and Python will happily sort, compare, and even do arithmetic-looking things with them until a comparison quietly lies.

Fix at the boundary: convert to `float` — or better, `Decimal` for money — when the response is parsed, so the rest of the program only ever sees numbers. Sorting is just where the lie became visible; the same strings would also break `max`, range filters, and sums (which would concatenate or TypeError). Type conversion is part of parsing, not an afterthought.

I unwrap the response with body['data'] and iterate it to process orders — but my loop runs exactly once, processing the string 'results' as if it were an order. The real orders are never touched and no error is raised. The envelope is nested deeper than I think. Show me what my loop actually iterated.

arguments.code:
body = {"data": {"results": [{"id": 1}, {"id": 2}, {"id": 3}],
                 "page": 1, "pages": 1}}

payload = body["data"]
print("type my loop received:", type(payload).__name__)
print("iterating it yields:", list(payload))
orders = body["data"]["results"]
print("the real orders:", orders, "| count:", len(orders))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
type my loop received: dict
iterating it yields: ['results', 'page', 'pages']
the real orders: [{'id': 1}, {'id': 2}, {'id': 3}] | count: 3

Your loop iterated a *dict*, and iterating a dict yields its keys — so it ran over `'results'`, `'page'`, `'pages'`, and your "processing" treated the string `'results'` as an order-like object. No error, because iterating a dict is legal; the code did something plausible with the wrong level of the envelope.

The real payload lives one level deeper: `body["data"]["results"]`, a list of 3 orders.

Envelope shapes (`data`, `results`, `items`, `payload.data`) differ per API and per endpoint, and being one level short fails *silently* whenever the intermediate value is iterable — dicts and strings both are. Defenses: assert the type you expect after unwrapping (`isinstance(x, list)`), and log the count of items extracted per response. A count of 3 that is really 'the envelope had 3 keys' is exactly the kind of coincidence a type assertion exists to catch.

My importer logs 'downloaded 500 records' and then processes 0. The response body in this client is a streaming iterator. I pass it to a logging helper first (which reads it to count bytes) and then to the parser. Both functions are correct in isolation. What happens between them?

arguments.code:
def fake_body():
    yield b'{"id": 1}\n'
    yield b'{"id": 2}\n'
    yield b'{"id": 3}\n'

body = fake_body()
logged_bytes = sum(len(chunk) for chunk in body)   # logger consumes the stream
print("logger counted bytes:", logged_bytes)
records = [line for line in body]                   # parser reads the SAME stream
print("parser received lines:", len(records))

body = fake_body()
chunks = list(body)                                  # buffer once...
print("buffered approach, parser lines:", len(chunks))

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
logger counted bytes: 30
parser received lines: 0
buffered approach, parser lines: 3

The stream was spent by the logger. A streaming body is an iterator: reading it advances it, and there is no rewind. The logging helper consumed all three chunks to count bytes — doing its job correctly — and handed the parser an exhausted iterator, which yields nothing, also correctly. Two right functions, one wrong composition: 500 downloaded, 0 processed.

The fix is to materialize once at the boundary: read the chunks into a list (or bytes) a single time, then let logging and parsing both work on the buffer. If the body is too large to buffer, restructure into a single pass that logs *while* parsing — one traversal, both jobs.

Any object whose type is an iterator (generators, streams, cursors) is single-use. When a pipeline shows 'fetched N, processed 0' with no error, look for a second consumer upstream — a logger, a validator, a `len()` — that drank the stream first.

Once in a while my JSON parsing fails with a decode error on an endpoint that 'returns JSON'. The failures correlate with errors elsewhere in the platform. I suspect the body is sometimes an HTML error page from a proxy. How do I prove what the body actually was, in code?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
200 application/json -> parsed as JSON
502 text/html -> NOT JSON; first bytes: <html><title>502 Bad Gateway</

Proven: when the platform has an incident, a proxy answers in HTML — status 502, content type `text/html` — and your parser throws the same `JSONDecodeError` you'd get from corrupt JSON. The error message blames the document; the document is fine, it is just not JSON and not from your API at all.

The general method: before parsing, record status and content type, and on parse failure, log the first bytes of the raw body. Those three facts separate every 'bad JSON' mystery into its real species — HTML error page, empty body, truncated body, wrong endpoint — in one log line.

Then branch properly: JSON parsing only for JSON content types, and treat a non-JSON response on a JSON endpoint as a transport-level failure (retryable when the status is 5xx). Parsers are bad diagnosticians; give them verified input and keep the raw evidence for yourself.

Two bugs reported against my client this week: (1) 'create reports failure but the widget exists afterwards' — the API returns 201 and my code checks status == 200; (2) 'delete crashes with a JSON decode error' — the API returns 204 and my code parses the body. Are these the same bug?

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
create, 201 -> FAILURE (but the widget was created)
delete, 204 -> JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)
success class is 2xx: True

Same family, two heads: your client encodes one exact success shape instead of the 2xx contract. Create returns **201 Created** — a success your `== 200` check reports as failure, while the side effect (the widget) happily persists, hence the 'lying' bug report. Delete returns **204 No Content** — success with an *empty* body by definition — and your unconditional `json.loads` crashes on the emptiness.

The fix is to branch on the class: any 2xx is success; parse a body only when one is expected (and present). 201 for creation and 204 for deletion are not API quirks, they are the standard's precise vocabulary.

Audit your client for both patterns: equality checks against 200, and parses that do not first ask whether a body exists. These bugs hide because the happy path (200 with JSON) is what most endpoints do most of the time — the endpoints that use the fuller status vocabulary find the assumptions.

My client occasionally fails to parse a response and logs show the JSON is cut off mid-string: '..."name": "widg'. The Content-Length header says 512 but the body I received is shorter. My code parses whatever arrived. What check am I missing?

arguments.code:
import json

raw = '{"name": "widg'
declared = 512
print("declared Content-Length:", declared)
print("bytes actually received:", len(raw.encode()))
try:
    json.loads(raw)
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print("parse error:", e.msg)
print("integrity check passes:", len(raw.encode()) == declared)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
declared Content-Length: 512
bytes actually received: 14
parse error: Unterminated string starting at
integrity check passes: False

You are parsing an incomplete body and letting the JSON parser report a transport problem in its own confusing dialect ("unterminated string" points at the text, not the connection). The response was truncated in transit — connection reset mid-body — and only a fragment of the declared 512 bytes arrived.

The missing check is integrity before parsing: compare received byte count against `Content-Length` when present (and treat a premature close on a chunked stream the same way). A mismatch means *transport failure*: retryable, loggable as such, and never the parser's problem.

This matters beyond cleanliness. Truncation mid-array can also produce *valid* JSON that is silently incomplete — a shorter list that parses fine. The length check (plus any server-provided total or checksum) is the only thing standing between you and quietly processing 80% of a dataset. Verify completeness first, parse second.

A partner API's JSON fails in my client with 'Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)' — but the body visibly starts with '{'. Their export tool writes the file with a BOM. My json.loads gets the raw text including the BOM character. Is char 0 really a brace?

arguments.code:
import json

raw = "﻿" + '{"total": 3}'
print("first character repr:", repr(raw[0]))
try:
    json.loads(raw)
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print("strict loads:", e.msg)
print("utf-8-sig decode ->", json.loads(raw.encode("utf-8").decode("utf-8-sig")))

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:
Char 0 is not a brace — it is U+FEFF, the byte-order mark, invisible in most logs and editors, which is why the body 'visibly starts with {' while the parser insists position 0 is invalid. Strict `json.loads` does not skip a BOM; the JSON grammar starts at the first real token.

Decoding the bytes as `utf-8-sig` strips the BOM when present and is harmless when absent, and the same text parses to the expected object.

BOMs ride in from Windows-side exporters, some partner feeds, and files that passed through certain editors. In the model, every call then succeeds, and refreshes happen at most once per TTL per process. Two guards: bound the refresh-retry to one attempt, or a genuinely revoked credential becomes an infinite auth loop; and make refresh single-flight in concurrent code, or five threads will refresh simultaneously and some providers invalidate all but the last token. Four of the five workers end up holding dead tokens and fail auth immediately after 'successfully' refreshing. The provider's counter tells the story: 5 refreshes for one expiry event.

The fix is single-flight refresh: one lock (per process, or a shared cache across processes), one worker refreshes, everyone else waits and then uses the shared result. The second model shows 1 refresh and zero failures.

B's call used: token-A (B never set a token)

The fix is structural: the token belongs to a client *instance* constructed per tenant, passed explicitly, with no global to fall back on — and a missing token should raise, not inherit. If a call can be made with a credential nobody set for this request, the design is the bug. Fail closed: no token, no request.

token scopes: ['read:orders'] | endpoint needs: write:orders

    return hmac.new(SECRET, data, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()

                                separators=(",", ":")).encode())
server_computed = sign(raw_body.encode())

print("server signs the received bytes   :", server_computed[:24], "...")

client signed the re-serialization: b846be85106edb0010753df6 ...
server signs the received bytes   : 6162288b1c9f50bcbeab2dfd ...
signatures match: False

Honoring the header, the second attempt lands at t=20, the window has reset, and it succeeds.

Note the subtlety in the model: the wait is not 'sleep 20 from the first failure' as a guess, it is the server's stated `Retry-After` — the limiter's own arithmetic, handed to you. Clients that ignore it are not being aggressive, they are being deaf. Implement: on 429 (and 503), read `Retry-After` (seconds or HTTP-date), wait that long (subject to your own maximum), and only then spend another attempt. Attempts are a budget; this bug spends the whole budget inside the penalty box.

Yours. The docs' 'limit: 100/min' on each page describes the *key's* budget as seen from that endpoint, not a private budget per endpoint. The server counts every request against one pool: 80 search + 80 billing = 160 against 100, so the last 60 get 429 — exactly when a job uses both endpoints in one minute, and never in single-endpoint tests, which is why it survived to production.

Rate limits are scoped by *something* — key, account, IP, endpoint, or a combination — and the scope is a contract fact you must establish, not infer from a docs page layout. The `X-RateLimit-*` headers on real responses usually name the scope honestly; check whether the remaining-count decreases across endpoints.

Client-side: keep ONE budget for the scope the server enforces (here, one bucket per key, shared by all endpoint callers in the process). Budgeting per endpoint against a pooled limit manufactures precisely the overage the limiter exists to prevent.

Every time we deploy, the API sees a burst from our service and we eat a wave of 429s in the first minute, then it settles. Our client-side limiter is in-memory. Deploys happen several times a day. Connect the dots with numbers: limit 60/min, 3 restarts in one minute during a rolling deploy.

arguments.code:

RESTARTS = 3         # rolling deploy restarts the process 3x in a minute
BURST_PER_START = 40 # queued work flushed at startup, under the fresh local limit

print("each fresh process sends:", BURST_PER_START, "(its new bucket allows it)")
print("server receives in that minute:", sent, "| limit:", LIMIT,

each fresh process sends: 40 (its new bucket allows it)
server receives in that minute: 120 | limit: 60 | rejected: 60

The limiter forgets, the server does not. Each restart creates a process with a fresh, full in-memory bucket, so each new instance happily flushes its 40 queued requests 'within limit'. Three restarts in a minute deliver 120 requests against the server's 60 budget: 60 rejections, every deploy, like clockwork. Between deploys the system looks perfectly behaved, which is why the correlation with deployments took time to spot.

Any in-memory limiter's real limit is `limit × restarts` over windows that contain restarts. Mitigations: persist the bucket state across restarts (shared store), start with an empty bucket and a warm-up ramp instead of a full one, or add startup jitter so the flush spreads out. The shared-store fix is the only one that makes the limit actually true.

General principle: client-side limits are statements about *aggregate* behavior, and aggregates do not reset just because your process did. If the state that enforces a promise lives and dies with the process, deploys are loopholes.

Our worker got stuck in a 429 loop for six hours without ever succeeding or failing the job. Looking at the code: the attempt counter increments inside the success branch, and the 429 branch sleeps and loops. The job framework's max_attempts is 8. Why did max_attempts never trip?

messages.content:
still looping after 21 iterations; attempts=0
gave up after 8 attempts

Because the counter guards a branch that never executes. `attempts` increments only on success, and success never comes — so `attempts < 8` is true forever, and the 429 branch loops without recording anything. The framework's safety limit exists but is wired to a counter the failure path never touches. Six hours of perfectly patient, perfectly useless retries.

The fixed version counts *every* attempt, incremented before the call regardless of outcome, and the job gives up after 8 as designed.

Retry loops need three independent bounds, all on the failure path: max attempts (counted per try, not per success), max total time (a deadline), and a backoff. Audit yours by asking: 'if the server returns 429 forever, what — in this code — ever stops?' If the honest answer is 'a human', the loop is unfinished. This is the retry cousin of the missing timeout: unbounded waiting dressed as resilience.

After the provider's API v2 upgrade, our welcome emails silently stopped: the sync runs fine, no errors, but every user record lands with an empty email. In v2 the field is called 'email_address'; my mapper reads 'email' with .get and a default of ''. Show me the silence, and how to make the next rename loud.

messages.name: code_runner

messages.content:

Silent defaults convert contract changes into data corruption.

The loud mapper declares the fields it requires from *this* API version and raises when they are missing: the next rename becomes an exception in the first minute, naming the missing field, instead of a month of un-sent email.

Rules for mapping layers: require the fields you depend on; default only fields that are genuinely optional in the contract; and count populated-ness ('records with an email: 0 of 3') as a sync health metric. Users see events shifted by 5 hours. Demonstrate the shift with real datetime math and give the parsing rule.

from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

raw = "2026-03-01T00:30:00"  # API means UTC, says nothing
naive = datetime.fromisoformat(raw)

as_local = naive.replace(tzinfo=ZoneInfo("America/New_York"))
print("buggy: stored as UTC ->", as_local.astimezone(timezone.utc))
as_utc = naive.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc)
print("right: stored as UTC ->", as_utc)

buggy: stored as UTC -> 2026-03-01 05:30:00+00:00
right: stored as UTC -> 2026-03-01 00:30:00+00:00

Five hours, exactly the Eastern offset — the timestamp was fine and the *interpretation* moved it. And push back upstream when you can: an API emitting naive timestamps is emitting ambiguity, and the correct long-term fix is offsets in the payload (`...Z` or `+00:00`). Until then, your parser owns the assumption — write it in one place, in the type itself (aware datetimes everywhere), so the guess can never be made twice.

Our order-status aggregator crashes about once a week with KeyError on a status it has never seen. The API added 'partially_refunded' to its status enum last month. My code maps every status through a fixed dict. Show the crash pattern and the tolerant design.

tolerant: ({'PAID': 2, 'SHIPPED': 1, 'OTHER': 1}, ['partially_refunded'])

The tolerant design treats unknown values as data, not exceptions: map what you know, bucket the rest under `OTHER`, and *report* the unknown values (here, `['partially_refunded']`) so a human can decide what they mean and extend the mapping deliberately.

The judgment call is per-consumer: an aggregator should be tolerant; a state machine that *acts* on status (release funds on 'paid') should be strict about the values it acts on and loud about the rest. What neither should do is crash mid-batch on a vocabulary word. Pin the known enum in a contract test that *alerts* on new values instead of a runtime that dies on them.

equals 1.00: True

integer cents sum: 2534 cents = 25.34

parsed %m/%d/%Y: 2026-03-04

Until then: never guess a slash format, and add a tripwire — if a parsed date disagrees with a related field (a weekday name, a timestamp), raise. My user import crashes on some records with TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable, at user['address']['city']. Most users have an address object; some have address set to null. null-safe: [('Ada', 'London'), ('Sam', 'UNKNOWN'), ('Kim', 'Seoul'), ('Jo', 'UNKNOWN'), ('Rex', 'Austin')]

Scattering `or {}` guards through business logic guarantees one call site will forget. And decide consciously what 'unknown' means downstream: for a shipping flow, an unknown city should *block* the record loudly, not flow through as a placeholder. buggy count: 3

parsed count: 1

Booleans deserve special suspicion because both spellings of wrongness (`"false"` truthy, `"0"` truthy) point the same way: toward over-counting whatever the flag gates — access, billing, activity.

Audit habit: for every numeric field you consume, write down its unit next to its type in your mapper. The fields that bite are never the exotic ones; they are money, weights (kg vs lb), durations (s vs ms), and sizes (bytes vs KB) — the mundane four.

Our exporter reads a very large response with b''.join(response.iter_chunks()) and the worker gets OOM-killed on big accounts. All the job actually needs is a count of records and a byte total. Show me the memory profiles of the two approaches on a stand-in stream — in counts, not wall-clock.

arguments.code:
def fake_chunks(n=1000, size=100):
    for _ in range(n):
        yield b"x" * size

# buggy: materialize everything, THEN measure it
chunks = list(fake_chunks())
total = sum(len(c) for c in chunks)
print("buffered: peak chunks held =", len(chunks), "| bytes counted =", total)

# streaming: fold each chunk into running totals, hold at most one
held, total, records = 0, 0, 0
for chunk in fake_chunks():
    held = 1
    total += len(chunk)
    records += chunk.count(b"\n")  # (stand-in payload has no newlines; count stays 0)
print("streaming: peak chunks held =", held, "| bytes counted =", total)

messages.name: code_runner
messages.content:
buffered: peak chunks held = 1000 | bytes counted = 100000
streaming: peak chunks held = 1 | bytes counted = 100000

The difference is not speed, it is *what the memory holds*: the buffered version peaks at 1,000 chunks — the entire response resident at once — while the streaming fold peaks at 1 chunk and produces the same byte total. Scale the stand-in to a real 1 GB export and the first version is an OOM kill, the second is unchanged.

The rule: if your processing is a *fold* (count, sum, hash, filter-write), stream it — never materialize a body just to reduce it. Materialization is only for when you genuinely need random access or multiple passes, and then it should be to disk, not RAM, at export scale.

OOM kills are especially confusing because the process dies without an exception to log. If workers die on 'big accounts' but never small ones, suspect a whole-body read (or a whole-result list) before suspecting the server. The fix is usually mechanical: iterate the stream, keep running state, write results incrementally.

My NDJSON importer parses each network chunk as complete lines. Depending on where chunks split, records break: a line arriving in two chunks fails to parse in both halves. The feed has 5 records; chunk boundaries fall mid-line twice. Show the failure and the buffered fix.

messages.content:
naive per-chunk parsing: ok, broken = (3, 4)
buffered line assembly : ok = 5

A record split across two chunks becomes two invalid fragments, so the naive version parses only the records that happened to align with chunk boundaries and errors on the rest. Worse, real chunk boundaries are chosen by TCP and proxies, so the failure count changes run to run with identical data.

The buffered parser keeps a remainder: append each chunk, extract only *complete* lines (up to a newline), and carry the partial tail into the next chunk. At end-of-stream, flush the remainder as the final line. All 5 records parse.

This remainder-buffer pattern is the whole of stream parsing — it recurs for CSV, for length-prefixed frames, for UTF-8 decoding. Any code that assumes 'one read = one message' is wrong on every streaming transport; messages must be reassembled from a byte stream whose segmentation is meaningless.

Our downloader resumes interrupted transfers by appending from the local file's length. Sometimes the resumed file is corrupt: longer than the original and failing checksum. def fake_download(range_from=None, honor_range=True):
    if range_from is not None and honor_range:
        return 206, ORIGINAL[range_from:]
    return 200, ORIGINAL  # server ignored Range: full body

partial = ORIGINAL[:40]                    # first attempt got 40 bytes, then dropped
status, rest = fake_download(range_from=len(partial), honor_range=False)
resumed = partial + rest                   # client appends blindly
print("status the client ignored:", status)
print("resumed length:", len(resumed), "| original:", len(ORIGINAL),
      "| content intact:", resumed == ORIGINAL)

status, rest = fake_download(range_from=len(partial), honor_range=True)
resumed = partial + rest if status == 206 else rest
print("with status check: length", len(resumed), "| intact:", resumed == ORIGINAL)

messages.content:
status the client ignored: 200
resumed length: 140 | original: 100 | content intact: False
with status check: length 100 | intact: True

The check is one comparison: only append when the response status is **206 Partial Content**. A 200 answer to a ranged request means 'here is the whole file' — restart from it, discarding the partial. Also verify the returned range/`Content-Length` against your expectation when offered.

Resume logic is a small state machine (fresh / resumed-206 / restarted-200 / complete), and the status code is its transition signal. Clients that treat the body as 'the rest of the file' without checking which response they actually got will corrupt files at exactly the rate their server ignores ranges — often only under load or via one CDN node, making it a maddeningly intermittent corruption.

My download progress bar crashes on some files (division by None) and on others sails past 250%. The code computes received / content_length * 100. Some servers omit Content-Length (chunked responses). Reproduce both symptoms and write the honest progress behavior.

honest, unknown total: 500 bytes (total unknown)
honest, known total  : 25%

Progress is a *display* of metadata, and metadata is optional in HTTP. Any computation over response headers must treat every header as possibly absent — `Content-Length`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, even on responses from your own company's API, because a proxy between you and it may strip or change them. Defensive display code is not paranoia; it is the protocol.

        for i in range(rows):
            produced += 1
            yield f"row-{i}\n"
    finally:
        print(f"server-side: generator closed after producing {produced} of {rows} rows")

server-side: generator closed after producing 1 of 10 rows
client believes it 'only read one row'

General principle: closing a stream early is a bandwidth optimization only. If the cost you care about is server compute, the request itself must ask for less. Clients that 'just read the first chunk' of an unbounded endpoint are exporting their preview feature's cost to the provider.

            queue -= 1                  # backpressure: producer waits / page not fetched yet
            consumed += 1
        if i % 2 == 1:
            queue -= 1                  # consumer processes 1 per 2 produced
            consumed += 1
        peak = max(peak, queue)
    return peak, consumed
